title: Search a 2D Matrix
statement: You are given a 2D grid of whole numbers called matrix, with ROWS rows and COLS columns, and a number called target.

Every row is sorted from left to right. The first number of each row is also bigger than the last number of the row above it, so reading left-to-right, row after row, the whole grid is one long sorted sequence.
Return True if target is anywhere in matrix, and False otherwise.
Your solution must be fast: it has to run in O(log(ROWS * COLS)) time. That rules out checking every cell one by one.

examples.explain: 3 sits at row 0, column 1. This is the example the visualizer runs. Watch the flat window l..r shrink, and its middle cell m jump around the grid.
13 falls in the gap between 11 and 16, so it's never in the grid and the window shrinks until it's empty.

pattern.name: Binary search over a flattened grid
pattern.summary: Because every row's first number is bigger than the row above's last number, reading matrix left-to-right, row after row, gives one sorted sequence, even though it's stored as rows. Pretend matrix is a single flattened list of length ROWS * COLS, binary search that list exactly like plain binary search, and convert whichever flat position you land on back into a real row and column with // and %.
recognize: A 2D grid where each row is sorted AND the rows are chained together: the last number of one row is smaller than the first number of the next.
The question only asks whether target exists somewhere in the grid, a single yes/no answer, not every matching cell or its exact position.
The required speed is O(log(ROWS * COLS)) or similar, ruling out checking every cell.
You could flatten the 2D structure into a 1D one mentally, without actually copying it, and binary search would still work on it.
avoid_when: Rows are individually sorted but NOT chained together (a number in row 2 could be smaller than a number in row 1). Then the grid isn't one sorted sequence, and plain binary search on it breaks; a row-by-row or staircase search is needed instead, like in Search a 2D Matrix II.
The grid is tiny. A plain nested loop is just as fast and harder to get wrong.
You need every matching cell, not just whether one exists.
The grid isn't sorted at all. There's nothing for binary search to use.

takeaways: The grid being sorted AND chained row-to-row is the only reason binary search applies: it's what makes the whole grid act like one long sorted list.

row, col = m // COLS, m % COLS is the standard way to turn a flat position back into a real grid position. m // COLS counts how many full rows come before m; m % COLS is how far into its own row m sits.
Everything else, the l <= r window, the m - 1 / m + 1 updates, is identical to plain binary search on a 1D list: this is the same algorithm, just with one extra conversion step.
This finishes in about log2(ROWS * COLS) steps: a grid with a million cells needs only about 20.
notes.time: O(log(ROWS * COLS)), logarithmic in the total number of cells. ROWS and COLS are the grid's dimensions. Doubling the grid's size adds just one more step.
notes.space: O(1), constant. Only ROWS, COLS, l, r, m, row and col, however big the grid is.
edge_cases: A 1x1 grid, like matrix = [[5]]. ROWS = COLS = 1, so l = r = 0 and the one cell is checked.

target not present but inside the overall range, like a number in the gap between two rows. The window shrinks all the way to empty and we return False, exactly like plain binary search with a missing target.
target smaller than every cell, or bigger than every cell. r ends at -1, or l ends at ROWS * COLS, and the loop exits cleanly without ever reading outside the grid.
A single row or a single column. COLS or ROWS is 1, and the flattening still works correctly either way.

1.explain: This creates a class named Solution, a container for related functions. LeetCode always wraps your answer in it.

syntax.meaning: A keyword meaning "I am defining a class".
The class name LeetCode looks for, with a capital S.
Ends the header. The indented block below belongs to the class.

1.why: LeetCode's tester creates a Solution object and calls your method on it.
1.if_removed: LeetCode can't find Solution and reports a NameError. A missing colon is a SyntaxError.

alternatives.difference: The older Python 2 style. In Python 3 it behaves exactly the same.

1.mistake: Lowercase class solution:. Capitalization matters to Python.
1.caption: Python reads the Solution blueprint. Nothing runs yet.

2.explain: This defines the method searchMatrix. It takes the 2D grid matrix and the number target, and promises to give back a boolean: True if target is somewhere in the grid, False otherwise.

syntax.meaning: Indentation: inside the class.
def starts a method definition. searchMatrix is the name LeetCode calls.
self is the Solution object, required as the first parameter of every method.
The grid, hinted as a List of List of int: a list of rows, each row itself a list of whole numbers.
The number to find, hinted as an int.
Return type hint: the answer is True or False.
Ends the header. The indented body follows.

2.why: LeetCode chooses the name and inputs. A True/False answer fits a yes/no question like "is target in the grid".
2.if_removed: Without self, the call crashes with a TypeError. Without the hints, nothing changes when the code runs.

alternatives.difference: No type hints. It runs identically.

2.mistake: Returning 1 or 0 instead of True or False. LeetCode expects an actual boolean here.
2.caption: Python remembers the searchMatrix instructions for later.

3.explain: This measures the grid. ROWS is how many rows matrix has, and COLS is how many numbers are in one row, read from matrix[0], the first row. Every row has the same length.

syntax.meaning: Indentation: inside the method.
Two variable names, assigned at once with tuple unpacking.
Assignment.
len gives how many items a list has. matrix is a list of rows, so this counts the rows.
Separates the two values: the first goes to ROWS, the second to COLS.
matrix[0] is the first row, itself a list of numbers. Its length is how many columns every row has.

3.why: Knowing ROWS and COLS lets the rest of the method treat the grid as one flattened list of ROWS * COLS numbers, without ever actually building that list.
3.if_removed: Line 4 would crash with a NameError, since ROWS and COLS wouldn't exist yet.

alternatives.difference: Two separate lines. Exactly the same result.

3.mistake: Writing len(matrix[0]) as len(matrix[1]), which breaks the moment the grid has only one row.
3.caption: matrix has {len(matrix)} row(s) and {len(matrix[0])} column(s) each.

4.explain: This sets up the search window as if matrix were one long sorted list. l starts at the first flat position, 0, and r starts at the last one, ROWS * COLS - 1.

syntax.meaning: Indentation: inside the method.
Two variable names for the left and right ends of the flat window, assigned together.
Assignment.
The first flat position of any grid.
Separates the two values: the first goes to l, the second to r.
The total number of cells, minus 1, since flat positions start counting at 0.

4.why: Both ends are INCLUSIVE, exactly like plain binary search on a list: l and r are real flat positions that are still candidates.
4.if_removed: The while loop on line 6 would crash with a NameError.

alternatives.difference: Two separate lines. Exactly the same result.

4.mistake: Forgetting the - 1, so r points one past the last real cell.
4.caption: The answer could be any of the {ROWS * COLS} cells: l = 0 and r = {ROWS * COLS - 1} cover all of them, read left-to-right, row after row.

6.explain: This loop keeps going as long as the flat window still has at least one candidate position left.

syntax.meaning: Indentation: inside the method.
A keyword that starts a loop which repeats its block for as long as the condition stays True.
<= means "less than or equal to". When l equals r, one cell is still left to check.
Ends the loop header.

6.why: Just like plain binary search on a 1D list, we don't know in advance how many halvings we need, so a while loop fits better than a for loop.
6.if_removed: Without the loop, only the very first middle position would ever be checked.

alternatives.difference: Misses a one-cell window: searchMatrix([[5]], 5) would never check the only cell.

6.mistake: Writing l < r with these inclusive bounds. The single-cell case is exactly what this bug breaks.

caption.text: l = {l} has passed r = {r}. The flat window is empty, so target isn't anywhere in the grid.

caption: The flat window from l = {l} to r = {r} covers {r - l + 1} cell(s). Keep searching.

7.explain: This finds the middle flat position of the current window, the same way plain binary search finds the middle index of a list.

syntax.meaning: Indentation: inside the while loop.
The variable for the middle flat position.
Assignment.
Start from the left end.
How far it is from l to r.
Integer division: divide and round DOWN to a whole number, since a flat position must be a whole number.

7.why: l + (r - l) // 2 never overflows in languages where numbers have a maximum size, unlike (l + r) // 2. Python's integers never overflow, but the habit carries over to other languages.
7.if_removed: Line 8 would crash with a NameError.

alternatives.difference: Simpler and perfectly safe in Python; gives exactly the same m.

7.mistake: Using / instead of //, which gives a decimal like 4.5 and later crashes when used as part of an index.
7.caption: The middle flat position of {l}..{r} is m = {l + (r - l) // 2}.

8.explain: This converts the flat position m back into a real cell: row is which row m falls in, and col is how far along that row m sits.

syntax.meaning: Indentation: inside the while loop.
Two variable names for the real grid position, assigned together.
Assignment.
Integer division: how many full rows of COLS cells fit before m, which is exactly m's row.
The remainder left over after those full rows: how far into that row m sits.

8.why: Flattening the grid into one long list is only conceptual; matrix is still really a list of rows. // and % together are the standard way to turn a flat position back into (row, col).
8.if_removed: matrix[row][col] on the lines below would crash with a NameError.

alternatives.difference: divmod does the // and % in one call and returns both as a pair. Exactly the same result, one built-in instead of two operators.

8.mistake: Swapping the two: row = m % COLS, col = m // COLS puts almost every position in the wrong cell.
8.caption: Flat position m = {m} is row {m // COLS}, column {m % COLS}.

10.explain: Compare the number at this cell with target. If the cell is BIGGER, target must come earlier in the flattened order, because the whole grid reads as one sorted sequence.

syntax.meaning: Indentation: inside the while loop.
Starts a condition. The block below runs only if it's True.
matrix[row] is that row (a list); adding [col] reaches into it for one number.
"Greater than" comparison.
The number we're looking for.
Ends the condition.

10.why: Because every row continues where the row above left off, the flattened grid is sorted. A too-big cell rules out every cell that comes after it too.
10.if_removed: Line 12's check would run on every pass, always shrinking the window in the same direction.

alternatives.difference: The same comparison written the other way round. Identical behaviour.

10.mistake: Getting the direction backwards: moving l when the cell is too big. The window then moves away from target.

caption.text: matrix[{row}][{col}] = {matrix[row][col]} is bigger than {target}, so target must come earlier in the grid.

caption: matrix[{row}][{col}] = {matrix[row][col]} isn't bigger than {target}.

11.explain: The cell was too big, so throw away flat position m and everything after it: move r to just before m.

syntax.meaning: Inside the if block.
Make r one flat position before m. The new window is l..m-1.

11.why: matrix[row][col] has already been ruled out as too big, so m itself is excluded too, with m - 1.
11.if_removed: The window never shrinks from the right, so the loop can run forever when target is earlier in the grid.

alternatives.difference: Keeps m in the window. With inclusive bounds and l <= r, this can loop forever.

11.mistake: Writing r = m. The classic infinite loop, same bug as in plain binary search.
11.caption: Discard flat position {m} (row {row}, col {col}) and everything after it: r moves from {r} to {m - 1}.

12.explain: Otherwise, check whether the cell is SMALLER than target. If so, target must come later in the flattened order.

syntax.meaning: Lines up with the if on line 10, so this elif belongs to it.
Short for "else if". Checked only if the if above was False.
< means "less than". Is this cell too small?
Ends the condition.

12.why: The mirror image of line 10. A too-small cell means every cell before it is even smaller, so they're ruled out too.
12.if_removed: Without this branch, a too-small cell would fall into else and wrongly be treated as a match.

alternatives.difference: A separate if instead of elif. Risky here, since it would still run its own check even after line 10's branch already changed r.

12.mistake: Using if instead of elif here, which can let both branches' logic interact in the wrong order.

caption.text: matrix[{row}][{col}] = {matrix[row][col]} is smaller than {target}, so target must come later in the grid.

caption: matrix[{row}][{col}] = {matrix[row][col]} isn't smaller than {target} either.

13.explain: The cell was too small, so throw away flat position m and everything before it: move l to just after m.

syntax.meaning: Inside the elif block.
Make l one flat position after m. The new window is m+1..r.

13.why: m has already been ruled out as too small, so it's excluded with + 1, guaranteeing the window shrinks.
13.if_removed: The window never shrinks from the left, so the loop runs forever when target is later in the grid.

alternatives.difference: Keeps m in the window. Can freeze the loop on a two-cell window.

13.mistake: Forgetting the + 1. It looks harmless but can freeze the method on a small window.
13.caption: Discard flat position {m} (row {row}, col {col}) and everything before it: l moves from {l} to {m + 1}.

14.explain: else catches the only remaining case: the cell is neither bigger nor smaller than target, so it must be EQUAL. We found it.

syntax.meaning: Lines up with the if and elif above. It's the last branch of the same chain.
"Otherwise": runs when every condition above was False.
Ends the line.

14.why: Not bigger and not smaller means equal, so there's no need to write the == check out.
14.if_removed: Without else, return True would run on every pass, whether the cell matched or not.

alternatives.difference: Spells out the equality. Clearer for some readers, but the check can never be False here, so it's redundant.

14.mistake: Misaligning else so it pairs with the wrong if.
14.caption: matrix[{row}][{col}] = {matrix[row][col]} equals {target}: found it!

15.explain: Give back True: target is somewhere in the grid, and we just found the exact cell.

syntax.meaning: Inside the else block.
End the method now, handing back True.

15.why: The question only asks whether target is in the grid, not where, so True is enough to answer it.
15.if_removed: The loop would keep going after finding target; since the else branch never changes l or r, it would loop forever.

alternatives.difference: Would hand back the position instead of a yes/no answer. Not what this problem asks for.

15.mistake: Returning matrix[row][col] instead of True. That's the number itself, not the yes/no answer.
15.caption: Return True: target {target} was found at row {row}, column {col}.

17.explain: The loop ended because the flat window became empty, so target is nowhere in the grid. Give back False.

syntax.meaning: Back at method level, after the loop. Only runs if the loop finished without returning.
Give back False, since no cell matched target.

17.why: Every cell was ruled out by the time l passes r, so target truly isn't anywhere in the grid.
17.if_removed: The method returns None when target is missing, which LeetCode marks wrong.

alternatives.difference: Another common "nothing found" signal in Python, but not what this problem asks for.

17.mistake: Putting return False inside the loop, where it would run after the very first comparison instead of after the search is over.
17.caption: The flat window is empty, so {target} isn't anywhere in the grid. Return False.

brute_force.explain: Check every cell, one row at a time, left to right, until target turns up. This works even if the grid weren't sorted at all.
brute_force.why_slow: In the worst case (target missing, or in the very last cell) this checks all ROWS * COLS cells. That's O(ROWS * COLS), and it completely ignores that every row continues where the row above left off.
brute_force.how_pattern_fixes: Because the flattened grid is sorted, binary search rules out half the remaining cells with a single comparison, finishing in O(log(ROWS * COLS)) steps instead of up to ROWS * COLS of them.
brute_force.time: O(ROWS * COLS): every cell may need checking.
brute_force.space: O(1): just the two loop variables.

glossary.algorithm: A step-by-step recipe for solving a problem. The same algorithm can be written in any programming language.
glossary.argument: The actual value you pass into a function when you call it.
glossary.assignment: Giving a name to a value with =. It's not a test for equality. That's ==.
glossary.Big O: A shorthand for how work or memory grows as the input grows. O(n) grows in step with the input. O(log n) barely grows. O(1) doesn't grow at all.
glossary.binary search: Searching a sorted sequence by repeatedly checking the middle and discarding the half that can't contain the target.
glossary.block: The group of indented lines under a line that ends with a colon (:).
glossary.brute force: Solving a problem in the most direct way, usually by checking everything. It's simple but often slow.
glossary.call: Running a function. You write its name followed by brackets with the arguments, like len(matrix).
glossary.class: A blueprint that groups related functions and data. LeetCode puts every answer in a class named Solution.
glossary.colon: The : character. At the end of a line like if, for, def or class, it means an indented block follows.
glossary.comparison operator: A symbol that compares two values and gives True or False: <, >, <=, >=, == and !=.
glossary.condition: An expression that is True or False, used by if, elif and while.
glossary.divmod: A built-in function, divmod(a, b), that gives both a // b and a % b at once, as a pair.
glossary.elif: Short for "else if". It checks another condition, but only when the if above it was False.
glossary.else (keyword): A keyword meaning "otherwise". Its block runs when every if or elif above it was False.
glossary.nested: Placed inside another of the same kind: a loop inside a loop, an if inside an if, or brackets inside brackets.
glossary.nested loop: A loop inside another loop. The inner loop runs completely for every single pass of the outer loop, so the work multiplies.
glossary.flattened: Treated as if a multi-row structure were laid out as one single long list, read in order.
glossary.for loop: A loop that runs its block once for each item in a collection, putting the item in a loop variable each time.
glossary.function: A named, reusable set of instructions you define with def and call by name.
glossary.inclusive: Including the end points. An inclusive window from 2 to 5 contains 2, 3, 4 and 5.
glossary.indentation: Spaces at the start of a line. In Python they decide which block a line belongs to.
glossary.index: A position in a list, counting from 0.
glossary.infinite loop: A loop whose condition never becomes False, so it runs forever and the program freezes.
glossary.integer: A whole number with no decimal point, like -1, 0 or 24.
glossary.integer division: Division that rounds down to a whole number, written // in Python. 7 // 2 is 3.
glossary.keyword: A word reserved by Python, like while, if, elif, else, return, for.
glossary.len: A built-in function that gives the number of items in a list: len([4, 8, 15]) is 3.
glossary.list: An ordered collection written with square brackets, like [1, 3, 5]. You reach items by their index.
glossary.logarithm: How many times you can halve a number before reaching 1. log2 of 1,024 is 10. That's why halving algorithms are so fast.
glossary.method: A function that belongs to a class or an object, called with a dot.
glossary.NameError: The error Python raises when you use a name that hasn't been assigned yet.
glossary.None: Python's value for "nothing". A function with no return statement gives back None.
glossary.object: A thing in memory that has a type and data, like a list or a Solution. Variables are names pointing at objects.
glossary.operator: A symbol that does something with values: + adds, - subtracts, // divides and rounds down, % gives the remainder, = assigns, < compares.
glossary.overflow: In some languages, numbers have a maximum size, and going past it wraps around to garbage. Python's integers grow as needed, so they never overflow.
glossary.parameter: A name in a function's definition that receives an input. matrix and target are searchMatrix's parameters.
glossary.pattern: A reusable technique that solves a whole family of problems.
glossary.pointer: A variable holding a position (here, a flat position) rather than the value stored there.
glossary.range: A built-in function that produces whole numbers. range(3) gives 0, 1, 2.
glossary.return: A keyword that ends a function and hands a value back to whoever called it.
glossary.self: The first parameter of every method. It refers to the object the method was called on.
glossary.sorted: Arranged in order, smallest to largest (ascending) unless stated otherwise.
glossary.sorting: Putting items in order. Sorting takes about O(n log n) time for a plain list.
glossary.space complexity: How much extra memory an algorithm needs as the input grows.
glossary.SyntaxError: The error Python raises when it can't read your code at all, for example a missing colon.
glossary.time complexity: How the running time grows as the input grows, written in Big O.
glossary.tuple: Like a list, but it can't be changed after it's made. It is written with round brackets, like (0, 1).
glossary.tuple unpacking: Assigning several names at once: l, r = 0, 9 puts 0 in l and 9 in r.
glossary.type hint: A label like target: int that tells readers what type a value should be. Python doesn't enforce it.
glossary.TypeError: The error Python raises when a value is the wrong type.
glossary.value: The part of a dictionary entry you get back, or more generally, any piece of data.
glossary.variable: A name that refers to a value, created with =.
glossary.window: The part of the search space that could still contain the answer, from l to r.

visualizer.title: matrix
visualizer.cursor: [row, col] if 'row' in globals() else None

marks.done: [[k // COLS, k % COLS] for k in range(ROWS * COLS) if k < l or k > r] if 'COLS' in globals() else []
